Ceremonies
sĕr´ē-mō-nĭz
n. pl. (the appointed outward forms of worship; rendering Hebrew chuqqah, statute, and mishpat, ordinance)
Latin caerimonia, a sacred rite. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, of the passover: kept “according to all the rites of it, and according to all the ceremonies thereof” (Num 9:3).

Biblical Definition

Ceremonies are the outward forms God appointed for the worship of the old covenant. Israel was to keep the passover “according to all the rites of it, and according to all the ceremonies thereof” (Num 9:3), and the first covenant “had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary” (Heb 9:1) which “stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation” (Heb 9:10). Paul gives their status now: “let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” (Col 2:16–17).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines ceremony as outward rite; external form in religion; the forms and rites prescribed by law or custom; outward forms of civility.

CEREMONY, n. Outward rite; external form in religion.

2. Forms of civility; rules established by custom for regulating social intercourse.

3. Outward forms of state; the forms prescribed or established by order or custom.

Key Scripture

Num 9:3 — "In the fourteenth day of this month, at even, ye shall keep it in his appointed season: according to all the rites of it, and according to all the ceremonies thereof, shall ye keep it."

Heb 9:1 — "Then verily the first covenant had also ordinances of divine service, and a worldly sanctuary."

Heb 9:10 — "Which stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation."

Col 2:16 — "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days:"

Col 2:17 — "Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ."

Modern Corruption

The ceremonies are either revived as though Christ had not come or despised as though God had never given them.

expand to see more

The Reformed have divided the law of Moses into moral, judicial and ceremonial, and the ceremonial law is the part the Confession says is now abrogated — not because it was bad but because it was a shadow, and the body is of Christ. Colossians 2:17 does not disparage the sacrifices, the feasts, or the priesthood; it dates them. A shadow is cast by something real and is exactly the shape of it, which is why the epistle to the Hebrews reads Leviticus with such attention. What has ceased is not their truth but their use, and to reinstate them — an altar, a priesthood, a sacrifice, a holy day binding the conscience — is to prefer the outline to the figure that cast it.

The opposite error empties Christian worship of form altogether, on the theory that ceremony as such belongs to the old covenant. It does not. The Lord left two ordinances with visible matter in them, water and bread and wine, and commanded that they be kept; He appointed a day, a table, a washing, and a book to be read and preached. The Reformed principle is not that worship should have no form but that its forms should be those God has appointed — which is why the Confession is at once so severe about invented ceremonies and so exact about the two that remain.

Hebrews 9:10 puts the limit of the whole system in one phrase: imposed on them until the time of reformation. The ceremonies could reach meats, drinks, and washings; they could not reach the conscience, which is what the next verses say the blood of Christ does. Every ceremonial religion since, Roman or Protestant, has failed at the same boundary, and the test of any observance is whether it is doing what only blood can do.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chuqqah (H2708), a statute, appointed thing; mishpat (H4941), ordinance, prescribed manner; Greek dikaioma (G1345), an ordinance; skia (G4639), a shadow.

expand to see more

Hebrew chuqqah (H2708) — statute, ceremony; Numbers 9:3, 9:12, 9:14, Exodus 12:14.

Greek dikaioma (G1345) — ordinance, carnal ordinance; Hebrews 9:1, 9:10, Luke 1:6.

Greek skia (G4639) — shadow; Colossians 2:17, Hebrews 8:5, 10:1.

Usage

"“According to all the ceremonies thereof” — the passover kept exactly."

"“Imposed on them until the time of reformation” — the system with a date on it."

"“A shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” — the outline and the figure."
